ab_juno_wall.blurb: A limestone sport wall beside the highway east of Jasper, bolted throughout and mostly one pitch long. Thirteen routes spread from 5.8 up to 5.11: a few easier lines, a trio around 5.9, and the bulk split between the 5.10 and 5.11 ranges, so it suits mid-grade climbers more than beginners. A marked trail of roughly a kilometre and a quarter climbs gently through forest to the base, finishing with a short, slightly exposed scramble. The open exposure warms the rock early in the year and dries it fast after rain, making spring and autumn the natural seasons, though wind can arrive suddenly. Bring a helmet, since loose rock sits near the base.

ab_air_voyage.blurb: A steep, overhanging quartzite wall forming the right flank of the big amphitheatre at the Back of the Lake, a short walk beyond the far end of Lake Louise. Thirteen routes mix eight trad lines with five bolted ones. Difficulty starts around 5.9 and climbs quickly: a small handful in the 5.11s, the largest share at 5.12, and a few at 5.13. The bolted classics sit mostly in the 5.11s while the harder gear routes reach the upper 5.12s, so this is a wall for climbers already comfortable at those levels rather than a place to learn.

ab_rock_gardens.blurb: A steep limestone sport crag in the forest close to Jasper townsite, facing northwest and generally shaded and out of the wind. The thirteen bolted single-pitch routes range from 5.7 to 5.12, with the heart of the crag in the 5.10s, a few easier warm-ups in the 5.7 to 5.8 range, and a couple of harder lines at 5.12. The rock is good quality and the faces are steep. The crag was once used for training by local mountaineers before being redeveloped for sport climbing. A walk of about ten minutes through Douglas fir leads in from the trail network, and a nearby second crag lies in the other direction at a fork.

ab_water_wall.blurb: The first wall you meet on the right when walking into Grotto Canyon near Canmore. The left side offers slabby, technical limestone, while the right side turns overhanging and favours power endurance, and that right side stays damp longer after wet weather. Of thirteen routes, eleven are bolted sport lines and two are aid. Grades run from 5.7 to 5.13, concentrated at 5.9 to 5.10 with a pair of 5.11s and two hard 5.13 lines, so there are a few friendly starters alongside the projects. The wall catches afternoon sun, and the polished rock typical of the canyon is part of the character.

ab_east_end_of_rundle_eeor.blurb: A big limestone face on the eastern end of Mount Rundle, towering over Canmore and reached by a steep hike of roughly half an hour to an hour from the road. Routes run from short single pitches to long multi-pitch lines of a dozen or more pitches. Of the thirteen routes here, most are trad, with a couple of aid lines and a couple of sport ones. Grades go from 5.7 to 5.11, with the majority in the 5.9 and 5.10 range, making it a realistic objective for solid intermediate parties. Rock quality varies, with cleaner stone higher up. Descent is usually by the hiking trail.

ab_upper_blackheart_amphitheater_convinc.blurb: A bolted ledge inside a large amphitheatre in Heart Creek, east of Canmore, with all thirteen routes being single-pitch sport climbs on good rock. The grade range runs from 5.8 to 5.13: one easy route, then a solid block of 5.11 and especially 5.12, and a pair at 5.13, which makes this a place for strong sport climbers. The elevated, exposed setting feels a little alpine, so it can run cooler than the creek below, and it pays to start early and carry an extra layer. Late spring through early autumn is the usual window.

ab_mind_games_wall.blurb: A sport wall on the right side of Black Feather Canyon in Banff National Park, reached by following the canyon drainage a good way upstream before it bends left. It sits opposite another wall and stays mostly shady through the day. The centrepiece is a patch of blue-grey rock with a pocked, brain-like texture and very good quality; steeper climbing is on the right and more vertical lines on the left. The wall is a bit shorter than its neighbours. All thirteen routes are bolted, mostly at 5.11 with a few at 5.12, two at 5.10 and one easy 5.7, so it is best for climbers in the 5.11 range.

ab_entrance_wall.blurb: The first wall on the right after you enter Carrot Creek canyon in Banff National Park, reached by a long, nearly level walk of about an hour that crosses the creek several times. A vertical face that grows taller as it runs upstream, it holds twelve bolted sport routes with a slick, sloper-friendly feel. Grades sit between 5.10 and 5.12, with most of the routes at 5.11 and a few at 5.10, so it is aimed at climbers who are already leading in the low 5.10s. It is considered less dramatic than the buttress further up the canyon but still has some good lines.
